subject: Biology
title: Cells Under the Microscope
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Cells Under the Microscope.

hook.text: In the 1670s, van Leeuwenhoek ground his own lenses and saw living things in a water drop.

buildup.text: He called them 'animalcules.' No one had seen single-celled life before.

discovery.text: Light microscopes reveal cells but can't resolve anything smaller than 200 nanometers.

twist.text: Electron microscopes shattered that limit, showing organelles in stunning detail.

climax.text: Modern cryo-EM can image individual proteins at near-atomic resolution.

punchline.text: Better lenses keep revealing smaller worlds.

quiz.question: What did van Leeuwenhoek call the organisms he saw under his microscope?

details.summary: Light microscopes reveal cell structure up to about 1,000x magnification, while electron microscopes achieve over 100,000x to reveal organelle ultrastructure. The invention of microscopy made cells visible for the first time and launched the entire field of cell biology.
details.whyItMatters: Everything we know about cells started with being able to see them. Advances in microscopy continue to drive biological discovery, from live-cell imaging to super-resolution techniques that visualize individual molecules.
takeaways: Light microscopes reveal cells and large organelles at up to 1,000x
Electron microscopes reveal ultrastructure at over 100,000x magnification
Fluorescence microscopy tracks specific molecules in living cells

faq.question: Why can't light microscopes see viruses?
faq.answer: Light microscopes are limited by the wavelength of visible light to resolving objects about 200 nanometers or larger. Most viruses are 20 to 300 nanometers, below or at this limit. Electron microscopes use shorter wavelengths to achieve the resolution needed.

faq.question: What did the 2014 Nobel Prize in Chemistry recognize?
faq.answer: The prize recognized super-resolution fluorescence microscopy, which broke the optical diffraction limit. Techniques like STED and PALM allow light microscopes to image structures smaller than 200 nanometers, bridging the gap between light and electron microscopy.
